newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma trial judge questions juror's seriousness.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma trial judge questions juror's seriousness.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial told a potential juror Friday he believed she had been "flip" when answering a detailed questionnaire and quizzed her closely on whether she could be a fair juror.

"Do you want to be on this jury?" U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch asked the woman. "Yes and no," she answered after admitting her 17-year-old son had told to "go for it" when her jury summons arrived.
"The impression I have is that you were kind of flip with your answers," when filling out a 40-page questionnaire last month, Matsch told her.

In several instances, the mother of two gave different answers in court than in the set of questions, which probed prospective jurors' opinions on a wide range of subjects including the death penalty and exposure to pre-trial publicity.

The judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys were trying to gauge prospective jurors' opinions before they are selected to decide the fate of Timothy McVeigh, accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
She said in court that she would consider eyewitness testimony about 30 percent reliable, after having written in her questionnaire she believed it to be 95 percent reliable.

As has been customary the judge did not announce whether the woman would be selected. The identity of the jurors has been kept secret and they sit behind a wooden screen out of the view of most spectators in the courtroom.

McVeigh, wearing a white shirt, was intent in the courtroom, listening closely to answers given by the prospective jurors. He has pleaded not guilty to the bombing and faces the death penalty if convicted.
Fifty-nine prospective jurors have been questioned in the 10 days since the trial began. Four of them have been eliminated publicly. Decisions on the others have not been announced.
One woman who had lived in Oklahoma City until 10 years ago said friends of hers who were nurses had set up emergency care stations near the bombing site.
Her other links to Oklahoma included a son in the Oklahoma National Guard and a visit to the site of the Murrah building on a recent trip to her home state.

About 15 years ago she served on a jury that sentenced a rapist-murderer to death. McVeigh's chief defence lawyer Stephen Jones asked her if she knew that the conviction had been overturned on appeal. She said she did not know.

The woman said she believed McVeigh was guilty and even after Jones asked her a series of rapid-fire questions showing that she had numerous ties to Oklahoma and the bombing, said she believed she could be fair.
